title: The Station That Saved New York's Landmarks
voice_direction: Measured, warm documentary delivery with a hint of gravity; let the hook land plainly, slow down and lower for the Times quote, a small dry beat on 'It didn't help', and a hushed, settled last line after the pause.
narration: New York saves its landmarks because of the one it lost. Pennsylvania Station, nineteen ten. A waiting room inspired by the baths of ancient Rome. In the sixties, the railroad agreed to replace it with Madison Square Garden. Architects picketed outside. It didn't help. On October twenty-eighth, nineteen sixty-three, the wrecking began. The New York Times wrote: [pause] "We will probably be judged not by the monuments we build but by those we have destroyed." Within two years, New York had a Landmarks Law. In nineteen seventy-eight, the Supreme Court upheld it, protecting Grand Central. And the old station? Much of it, statues included, went to a landfill in the New Jersey Meadowlands. One statue, called Night, was pulled back out. It stands in Brooklyn now. The rest, as far as anyone knows, is still out there. [pause] Under the marsh.

instagram_caption:
Pennsylvania Station opened in 1910. Designed by McKim, Mead & White, its waiting room was inspired by the Baths of Caracalla in Rome, under a ceiling 150 feet high.

In the early 1960s the railroad agreed to tear it down so a new Madison Square Garden could be built on the site. On 2 August 1962 architects, Philip Johnson among them, picketed outside. It didn't help. Demolition began on 28 October 1963.

Two days later The New York Times wrote: "we will probably be judged not by the monuments we build but by those we have destroyed."

On 19 April 1965 Mayor Robert F. Wagner signed New York City's Landmarks Law and created the Landmarks Preservation Commission. In 1978 the U.S. Supreme Court upheld that law in Penn Central v. New York City, and a tower was kept off Grand Central Terminal.

And the old station? The Brooklyn Museum says Adolph Weinman's facade sculptures were carted to a landfill in the New Jersey Meadowlands along with the rest of the rubble. One figure, "Night", was retrieved and now stands in the museum's sculpture garden. How much of the rest still lies in the marsh, nobody can say for sure.

facts.claim: The original Pennsylvania Station, designed by McKim, Mead & White, opened in 1910
facts.source: Brooklyn Museum, 'Remembering Penn Station' (BKM Tech blog, 8 Sep 2010); Wikimedia Commons category description

facts.claim: Its waiting room, with a 150-foot ceiling, was inspired by the Roman Baths of Caracalla (and the Basilica of Constantine)
The above-ground station was demolished so Madison Square Garden / Pennsylvania Plaza could be built on the site
facts.source: NYU / New-York Historical Society, Alexander Hatos Photograph Collection finding aid (chronology); NYC City Planning Commission report on Penn Station / MSG

facts.claim: On 2 August 1962 architects (Action Group for Better Architecture in New York), including Philip Johnson, picketed outside Penn Station
facts.source: Landmark West!, 'The History of Preserving History: Penn Station Rally 50 Years Later'; AIA New York (Oculus)
Landmark West!; NYU/N-YHS Hatos finding aid ('demolition ... commences in October 1963')

facts.claim: NYT editorial 'Farewell to Penn Station', 30 Oct 1963, p. 38: 'we will probably be judged not by the monuments we build but by those we have destroyed'
facts.source: The New York Times, 30 October 1963 (ProQuest Historical Newspapers), as quoted consistently by Commonweal, History News Network and others. Original not opened in this session

facts.claim: Mayor Robert F. Wagner signed the Landmarks Law, creating the Landmarks Preservation Commission, on 19 April 1965
The Landmarks Law was a response to the public outcry over the loss of Pennsylvania Station
facts.source: New York City Council Res. 0922-2005; NYC LPC 50th-anniversary materials

facts.claim: Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City, 438 U.S. 104, decided 26 June 1978 (6-3), upheld the Landmarks Law as applied to Grand Central, after the LPC refused an office tower above the terminal
Weinman's facade sculptures were carted to a landfill in the New Jersey Meadowlands along with the rest of the rubble
Weinman's 'Night' clock figure (c. 1910) was retrieved from landfill in the New Jersey Meadowlands and is in the Brooklyn Museum (66.250.1), displayed in the Steinberg Family Sculpture Garden
Penn Station debris went to the Meadowlands, focused on a truck yard at the edge of Secaucus; remains recovered there, but it is hard to say for sure what came from the station
facts.source: Center for Land Use Interpretation, 'Penn Station Burial Grounds'
